# Family saga and social-drama lens

Apply to narratives centered on families, communities, institutions, or social relationships across extended time. Emphasize inheritance, loyalty, power, and change without assuming that every family story is a saga.

## Chapter-level prompts

- Track the relevant family/community unit, generation, time period, and shifts in point of view. Note time jumps and the information they leave out.
- Record relationships and roles (care, dependence, conflict, obligation, chosen kinship) as the text presents them; distinguish formal status from emotional reality.
- Follow the transfer or contest of resources and power: property, labor, status, knowledge, caregiving, authority, or reputation.
- Identify the public/social pressure influencing private choices, including class, migration, race, religion, gender roles, institutions, and local norms when textually relevant.
- Track secrets, inherited stories, silences, and repeated behavior without assuming that descendants simply reproduce ancestors.
- Note a chapter's change to family alliances, household structure, communal standing, or generational understanding.

## Whole-work prompts

- Map generational or community arcs and show how earlier decisions constrain or enable later ones, with chapter references.
- Analyze continuity and change in family patterns, traditions, power, memory, and belonging; identify breaks as well as repetition.
- Assess how the narrative's time scale and viewpoint distribution shape whose experience becomes central or peripheral.

## Guardrails

- Do not reduce a family to a single symbolic role or assume biological ties define relationships.
- Avoid unsupported diagnoses or moral verdicts; describe actions, consequences, and narrative framing.
- Distinguish verified social/historical context from the work's fictional depiction.
